subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hypertension: primary, secondary, urgency vs emergency
vignette: A 44-year-old man is evaluated at two separate clinic visits 3 weeks apart. His blood pressure readings are 138/86 mm Hg and 142/88 mm Hg. He reports no headaches, visual changes, or chest pain. Physical examination is unremarkable, and basic laboratory studies are normal.
question: Which of the following criteria establishes a diagnosis of hypertension in this patient?

options.text: Sustained systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥90 mm Hg
Persistent systolic BP ≥130 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥80 mm Hg
A single systolic BP reading ≥130 mm Hg on any one occasion
Systolic BP ≥180 mm Hg together with diastolic BP ≥120 mm Hg
Systolic BP ≥150 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥95 mm Hg

explanation_correct: Hypertension is defined as persistent systolic blood pressure ≥130 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥80 mm Hg. This patient's readings of 138/86 and 142/88 mm Hg exceed the 130/80 threshold on repeated measurements, establishing the diagnosis. The 'and/or' construction means an elevation of either systolic or diastolic pressure alone is sufficient, and persistence (not a single reading) is required.

explanation_incorrect.A: ≥140/≥90 mm Hg was the threshold in older classification systems, but the current definition used on examinations is ≥130 and/or ≥80 mm Hg; using 140/90 would delay diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: A single elevated reading is not diagnostic; hypertension requires persistent elevation confirmed on repeated measurement.
explanation_incorrect.D: ≥180/≥120 mm Hg defines severe hypertension, which raises the question of hypertensive urgency or emergency, but it is not the threshold for diagnosing hypertension generally.
explanation_incorrect.E: ≥150/≥95 mm Hg is an arbitrary, outdated threshold that is far above the current definition and would miss the large majority of hypertensive patients.

educationalObjective: Recall that hypertension is persistent systolic BP ≥130 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥80 mm Hg.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hypertension: primary, secondary, urgency vs emergency
vignette: A 34-year-old woman is found to have a blood pressure of 168/104 mm Hg on three occasions over 2 months. The hypertension has been difficult to control despite two antihypertensive agents. Auscultation of the abdomen reveals a bruit. Serum potassium is 4.2 mEq/L and renal function is normal. Renal angiography demonstrates alternating areas of stenosis and dilation of the right renal artery.
question: What is the most likely cause of this patient's hypertension?

options.text: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis
Obstructive sleep apnea
Primary (essential) hypertension
Fibromuscular dysplasia
Primary hyperaldosteronism

explanation_correct: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a cause of renovascular hypertension characterized by a 'string of beads' appearance of the renal artery on angiography, produced by alternating stenoses and dilations. It is classically seen in adult females and is one of the most common causes of the 10% of hypertension that is secondary to renal/renovascular disease. The abdominal bruit reflects turbulent flow through the stenotic renal artery.

explanation_incorrect.A: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis typically occurs in older patients with other vascular disease and produces a single focal stenosis rather than the alternating stenoses and dilations ('string of beads') seen here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Obstructive sleep apnea is a recognized cause of secondary hypertension, but this patient has no history of snoring, apneic episodes, or obesity, and the angiographic finding points to renal artery disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: Primary (essential) hypertension accounts for 90% of cases, but the young age of onset, resistance to two drugs, abdominal bruit, and abnormal angiography all indicate secondary hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Primary hyperaldosteronism classically presents with hypertension and hypokalemia; this patient's potassium is normal and her angiography shows renal artery disease instead.

educationalObjective: Recognize the 'string of beads' angiographic appearance of fibromuscular dysplasia as a cause of secondary hypertension in young adult women.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hypertension: primary, secondary, urgency vs emergency
vignette: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a severe headache and blurred vision of several hours' duration. Her blood pressure is 204/124 mm Hg. She is disoriented to place and time. Funduscopic examination shows retinal hemorrhages and exudates with papilledema.
question: Which of the following best describes this patient's condition?

options.text: Hypertensive emergency, defined by evidence of acute end-organ damage
Hypertensive urgency, which can be managed with oral agents over 24–48 hours
Hypertensive urgency, because retinal findings are chronic and asymptomatic
Primary (essential) hypertension, appropriate for outpatient follow-up
Secondary hypertension due to renal artery stenosis, requiring only outpatient workup

explanation_correct: A hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (≥180/≥120 mm Hg) with evidence of acute end-organ damage. This patient's encephalopathy (disorientation), retinal hemorrhages and exudates, and papilledema are classic examples of acute end-organ damage listed for hypertensive emergency. In emergencies, arterioles may show fibrinoid necrosis, and treatment requires prompt parenteral blood pressure lowering rather than outpatient management.

explanation_incorrect.B: Hypertensive urgency is severe hypertension (≥180/≥120 mm Hg) without acute end-organ damage; this patient has encephalopathy and retinopathy, making this an emergency rather than an urgency.
explanation_incorrect.C: The retinal hemorrhages, exudates, and papilledema are acute manifestations of hypertensive end-organ damage, not chronic incidental findings; their presence rules out urgency.
explanation_incorrect.D: Outpatient management of primary hypertension is inappropriate for a patient with acute end-organ damage; this presentation demands emergent treatment.
explanation_incorrect.E: Although secondary causes should be sought later, the immediate issue is the acute end-organ damage, which makes this a hypertensive emergency requiring inpatient management.

educationalObjective: Distinguish hypertensive emergency (severe hypertension WITH acute end-organ damage such as encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhages/exudates, or papilledema) from hypertensive urgency (severe hypertension WITHOUT end-organ damage).

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hypertension: primary, secondary, urgency vs emergency
vignette: A 58-year-old man with a 15-year history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with progressive exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography shows marked thickening of the left ventricular wall with a normal chamber cavity size and preserved ejection fraction. He has no history of valvular disease or infiltrative disease.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the myocardial response to this patient's chronic hypertension?

options.text: Eccentric hypertrophy with sarcomeres added in series, due to chronic volume overload
Concentric hypertrophy with sarcomeres added in series, causing cavity dilation
Concentric hypertrophy mediated by angiotensin II and endothelin
Ischemic dilation with thinning of the left ventricular wall
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy caused by a sarcomere gene mutation

explanation_correct: Chronic pressure overload from hypertension predisposes to concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, in which sarcomeres are added in parallel and the wall thickens while the chamber cavity remains normal in size — exactly what this patient's echocardiogram shows. This hypertrophic response is mediated by angiotensin II and endothelin. Hypertension also predisposes to CAD, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Eccentric hypertrophy with sarcomeres added in series is the response to volume overload (eg, valvular regurgitation), producing a dilated, thin-walled ventricle — not the thick-walled, normal-cavity ventricle seen in pressure overload.
explanation_incorrect.B: Concentric hypertrophy is correct in name, but sarcomeres are added in parallel (not in series) in pressure overload, and it does not cause cavity dilation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thinning and dilation of the left ventricular wall describes a dilated (ischemic or idiopathic) cardiomyopathy, not the compensatory response to hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy from a sarcomere mutation is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a genetic disease, not the adaptation to chronic pressure overload.

educationalObjective: Recall that chronic hypertension causes concentric LVH mediated by angiotensin II and endothelin.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Hypertension: primary, secondary, urgency vs emergency
vignette: A 49-year-old obese man is evaluated for blood pressures of 172-185/100-112 mm Hg despite three maximally dosed antihypertensive agents. His wife reports loud nightly snoring with witnessed apneic episodes, and he describes excessive daytime sleepiness. He is a non-smoker and does not use NSAIDs. Serum potassium is 4.3 mEq/L, creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, no abdominal bruit is heard, and urinalysis is unremarkable.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's resistant hypertension?

options.text: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery
Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis
Primary hyperaldosteronism
Primary (essential) hypertension with nonadherence to medications
Obstructive sleep apnea

explanation_correct: Obstructive sleep apnea is one of the most common causes of the roughly 10% of hypertension that is secondary, and it is a classic cause of resistant hypertension. The vignette's hallmarks — obesity, loud snoring with witnessed apneas, and daytime somnolence — point directly to OSA. Treating the apnea can dramatically improve blood pressure control. Renovascular and aldosterone-related causes are excluded by the normal potassium, creatinine, and absent bruit.

explanation_incorrect.A: Fibromuscular dysplasia classically affects young adult women and would be expected to produce an abdominal bruit and a 'string of beads' angiogram; neither is present here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis would typically occur in an older patient with known atherosclerotic disease and an audible abdominal bruit, which is absent in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.C: Primary hyperaldosteronism characteristically produces hypokalemia; this patient's potassium is normal and he has no features suggesting mineralocorticoid excess.
explanation_incorrect.D: While nonadherence is a common reason for apparent resistance, the vignette gives a specific secondary cause with strong supporting features (snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime somnolence) that must be addressed.

educationalObjective: Include obstructive sleep apnea in the differential of secondary hypertension, especially in obese patients with snoring, witnessed apneas, and resistant hypertension.
